https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ce973y.text: Nine killed in strikes on Kyiv, as Ukraine sinks Russian container ship 1 August 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Chris Graham Moscow has been escalating deadly ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine's capital At least nine people have been killed and dozens injured in Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Moscow has escalated deadly ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv recently, prompting Zelensky to say that missile interceptors are urgently needed. The strikes come two days after a suspected Russian cruise missile landed in Poland during a widespread attack on Ukraine that killed at least eight people, including six members of one family. Separately, Ukrainian drones sank a Russian-owned container ship in the Black Sea on Saturday. Moscow said all 17 crew were rescued. Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the capital had come under a ballistic missile attack on Saturday, with AFP reporting more than 10 explosions. Fires broke out across the city and power cuts were reported in some areas. Klitschko said a residential building in Shevchenkivskyi was partially destroyed, trapping people inside. The emergency services said at least seven people were killed in a strike in the Darnytskyi district. Another 14 were injured, including two children, it reported. In Solomyanskyi district, two people died and eight were injured, including two children, as a five-storey residential building was partially destroyed, officials said. A missile landed near the Lithuanian embassy, breaking windows and scattering debris in the compound, Lithuania's foreign ministry said. Reuters Zelensky said in a post on X that the sanctioned 100,000-tonne capacity container ship Yanina had been "sent to the bottom". Moscow confirmed the attack in a statement from state-owned nuclear operator Rosatom, which owns the ship. Rosatom said it had been transporting civilian goods including frozen food and construction materials, adding that the attack took place 130 miles (209km) from Novorossiysk. "Such an attack cannot be interpreted as anything other than piracy and robbery," Rosatom's CEO Alexey Likhachev said, adding that all 17 crew members were in a "satisfactory" condition. Ukraine has targeted Russian-flagged ships in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion of the country in 2022. The attack on Kyiv comes after Zelensky met President Donald Trump in Washington DC earlier this week to urge the US to grant Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot interceptor missiles. Asked about the missiles during a cabinet meeting at the Camp David retreat on Friday, Trump said the US had not agreed to Ukraine building Patriot missiles but that talks were ongoing. He said the US had to be "very careful about letting somebody build them". Emphasising concerns about sharing advanced US weaponry, Trump called it "a big step". Trump's latest comments regarding Patriot missiles come weeks after he offered to give Ukraine the right to produce them. As Russia has stepped up its air attacks, Ukraine has run low on supplies of Patriots, which remain the only weapon in its arsenal capable of downing ballistic missiles. "I don't think this would ever happen, but, you know, those people that you give that technology, they can someday turn on you," Trump said. Zelensky said in a post on X on Friday that he had followed up on his meeting with Trump with a "good" phone call with US Vice-President JD Vance. "As Russia's air attacks on our country continue unabated, air defence – specifically Patriot interceptors against ballistic missiles – remains a top priority," Zelensky wrote. For its part, Ukraine has escalated its retaliatory strikes in recent months, including attacks on several retail warehouses belonging to Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries. Kyiv says it is targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army. Andreas Thom, Professor of Geometry at TU Dresden, suspects that unpublished research content from his ChatGPT conversations may have been incorporated into the training of OpenAI models. This could potentially have contributed to another mathematical breakthrough that OpenAI presented in early August. Continue after ad According to the company, an internal version of Astra had, for the first time, answered a central question in group theory. The proof significantly builds on earlier work by mathematician Gábor Kun from the Alfréd-Rényi Institute in Budapest, as well as on joint work by Kun and Thom. Thom found it suspicious that Astra pursued this particular line of research, even though, according to his account, it was not considered the most obvious solution path. Thom demands transparency on data usage As Thom writes on Mastodon , he had previously spent months actively discussing ongoing research questions with a colleague in Dresden using ChatGPT. Following OpenAI’s August announcement , Thom asked OpenAI researchers Mark Sellke and Sébastien Bubeck two questions: Firstly, whether content from these conversations had been included in training data, and secondly, whether the conversations had been accessible to the AI system during its search for the proof. According to Thom, Sellke merely replied, “Regarding your conversations with ChatGPT: that did not happen.” Videos by heise mehr Videos c't 3003 heise & ct Peertube In retrospect, Thom considers precisely this answer to be “unjustifiably broad and materially misleading.” In the Navier-Stokes controversy, OpenAI now explicitly distinguishes between the two cases: the company stated that the researchers and AI agents involved had not accessed specific user data from mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge. At the same time, however, OpenAI cannot rule out that de-identified data from their previous use of ChatGPT may have contributed to improving the models. Continue after ad Thom now demands more transparency: If OpenAI denies his questions broadly, the company must disclose which data, model versions, and account settings this claim is based on. According to his statements, Thom deactivated the use of his content for model training on June 29. However, this leaves open what happened previously with older conversations or data already derived from them. Furthermore, it is not possible to verify from the outside how this setting is technically implemented. “If nonpublic research supplied by users improved a model and the provider then used that model to race those users to publication - without informed consent, disclosure, or credit - that would be ethically indefensible,” writes Thom. De-identification can remove a name but not the intellectual content of a mathematical idea. OpenAI adds sources after criticism In addition to the fundamental questions of data protection and technical traceability of previous training and usage data, there is further criticism of OpenAI’s handling of scientific prior work. Mathematician Gonzalo Cao-Labora pointed out on X that the original Navier-Stokes paper was missing several relevant works in its bibliography, accusing OpenAI of not adequately acknowledging previous research. A few hours later, OpenAI added several sources and a paragraph linking previous research approaches to its own Navier-Stokes proof. Even after these additions, Cao-Labora still considered the contextualization of prior work to be insufficient. ( mho ) Don't miss any news – follow us on Facebook , LinkedIn or Mastodon . Photograph: Roger Anis/AP Egypt Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Peter Beaumont Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.16 EDT Last modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country. Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt. According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups. “Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP. Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added. The news website that’s keeping press freedom alive in Egypt | Leslie T Chang Read more Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions. Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood. Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom. View image in fullscreen Lina Attalah holds a meeting in the Mada Masr office in 2015. Photograph: Sabry Khaled/Sabry Khaled For The Guardian The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing. “This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.” According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi , since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”. Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”. Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November. Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves. “Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.” Explore more on these topics Egypt Press freedom Middle East and north Africa Africa Newspapers & magazines Human rights news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained Two Romanians jailed over stabbing of Iranian TV journalist in London UK state threats bill could pull British journalists into terror prosecutions, experts say Journalist detained in Kuwait acquitted of ‘spreading false information’, says press monitor Israel responsible for two-thirds of record 129 press killings in 2025, says CPJ BBC journalist barred from leaving Vietnam and interrogated repeatedly Italian investigative journalism TV host targeted in bomb attack near Rome UN and rights groups condemn reported jailing of Wuhan Covid citizen journalist Zhang Zhan: who is the Chinese citizen journalist facing a second trial?
